results.result: The YellowCaB mouse model was successfully generated by crossing ROSA26-TN-XXL mice with CD19-Cre mice, resulting in exclusive expression of the calcium indicator TN-XXL in CD19+ B lymphocytes. The expression was confirmed by confocal microscopy and flow cytometry, with no differences observed between heterozygous and homozygous mice, or between male and female mice. Cell numbers were comparable to wild-type controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35, C39-C45, and C53 are well-supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 1a,b), flow cytometry (Figure 1c), and cell count data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The breeding strategy is clearly described, and the specificity of TN-XXL expression to CD19+ cells is demonstrated. The lack of differences between genotypes and sexes is appropriately documented.

results.result: The TN-XXL calcium indicator responds to ionomycin stimulation with a steep increase in FRET signal, reaching 50-55% ΔR/R over baseline. Approximately three-quarters of cells showed detectable FRET responses, with the majority exhibiting 35-40% signal change. A threshold of 20% ΔR/R was established for positive responsiveness based on the bimodal distribution of responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C46-C52 are supported by flow cytometry (Figure 1d) and confocal imaging data (Figure 1f,g). The calcium-dependence was independently validated using X-Rhod-1 dye (C47). The threshold definition (C52) is based on observed bimodal distribution in the histogram. Sample sizes (>100 cells) are adequate for the characterization.

results.result: BCR stimulation with anti-IgM F(ab)2 fragments induces dose-dependent calcium responses in YellowCaB cells, with saturation at 10 µg/ml. The FRET signal peaks at >30% ΔR/R and lasts over 3 minutes, followed by a residual signal of ~7% for an additional 3.5 minutes. B cells can be repeatedly stimulated under continuous perfusion conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C56-C62 are supported by dose-response experiments (Figure 2a,b) showing concentration-dependent calcium responses. The repeated stimulation capability (C62) is demonstrated by multiple FRET peaks under perfusion. The residual signal observation (C60-C61) is clearly documented, though the interpretation about calcium storage (C61) is somewhat speculative but reasonable.

results.result: Stimulation of the BCR light chain with anti-kappa antibody induces calcium increases in YellowCaB cells, but with a differently shaped FRET peak and requiring higher antibody concentrations (>150 µg/ml) compared to heavy chain stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a. The observation of different response characteristics between light and heavy chain stimulation is documented, though the mechanistic basis for these differences is not explored.

results.result: Anti-CD40 treatment alone does not induce calcium responses, but pre-treatment with anti-CD40 modifies subsequent BCR-stimulated calcium responses into three distinct patterns: sustained, transient, or intermediate. Sustained flux can saturate the sensor at levels comparable to ionomycin, while cells showing intermediate flux retain the ability to respond to ionomycin.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2c showing distinct calcium flux patterns after CD40 pre-treatment. The characterization of three response types is clearly documented, and the sequential stimulation with ionomycin validates that intermediate responders retain sensor capacity.

results.result: TLR stimulation modulates BCR-induced calcium responses. TLR9 stimulus (CpG) alone has no effect on FRET levels but delays the subsequent BCR-stimulated FRET peak. TLR4 stimulation (LPS) induces minor calcium elevation alone and decreases BCR-stimulated FRET levels when applied before BCR stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2d,e showing the effects of TLR stimulation on calcium dynamics. The differential effects of TLR9 (delay) versus TLR4 (attenuation) on BCR responses are clearly documented, though the mechanistic basis is not fully explored.

results.result: B cells can collect and integrate multiple BCR-induced calcium signals for full activation, with signaling patterns shaped by innate signals or T cell help. BCR inhibition abolishes FRET responses to anti-IgM, while CXCL12 stimulation produces no detectable FRET peak, likely due to insufficient sensor sensitivity for small calcium changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 are supported by the repeated stimulation experiments (C75-C76), BCR inhibition data (C77, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), and CXCL12 testing (C78, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d). The conclusion about signal integration (C75-C76) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the speculation about CXCL12 sensor sensitivity (C78) is acknowledged as such.

results.result: Intravital two-photon imaging demonstrates that adoptively transferred YellowCaB cells migrate into germinal centers and exhibit traceable calcium fluctuations. FRET intensity fluctuates around low levels in moving cells, while sustained increases require cell arrest, with some cases showing sustained elevation after prolonged cell-cell contacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by histological confirmation (Figure 3a), intravital imaging data (Figure 3b, Video 1), and movement analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The correlation between cell arrest and sustained calcium elevation (C84) is supported by both the current data and cited literature (Negulescu et al., 1996; Shulman et al., 2014).

results.result: Analysis of B cell-FDC contacts reveals that transient B cell-FDC contacts are followed by gradual increases in cytoplasmic calcium concentration, while cells maintaining strong FDC contact sustain elevated calcium levels. A threshold of 150 AU colocalization intensity was established to distinguish strong from transient contacts based on biexponential fit decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by colocalization analysis (Figure 3c) and single-cell tracking data (Figure 3d). The threshold definition (C85) is based on quantitative analysis of the colocalization intensity distribution. The correlation between FDC contacts and calcium increases (C86-C88) is clearly demonstrated, though causality (C88) is inferred rather than directly proven.

results.result: The FLIM approach for calcium quantification is tissue depth-independent, as demonstrated by consistent measurements at different depths (100, 130, 160 µm). The TCSPC system was validated using SHG and eGFP standards, which showed expected phasor positions, confirming that no data correction is necessary.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C91, C97-C99, C102, C150 are supported by validation experiments (Figure 4a) and depth-independence testing (Figure 4f). The technical advantage of FLIM over ratiometric methods in avoiding photobleaching and scattering artifacts (C150) is well-established. The validation with reference standards (C97-C99) is appropriate and demonstrates system reliability.

results.result: The TN-XXL sensor was calibrated using lysate titrations, yielding Kd = 475 ± 46 nM and Hill slope = -1.43 ± 0.17. The phasor-based calibration strategy from Celli et al. (2010) was adapted for TN-XXL in B lymphocytes. The dynamic range spans 100 nM to 4 µM free calcium, with a linear range of 265-857 nM. Time-domain and phase-domain approaches showed <5% deviation.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33, C100-C101, C104-C106, C155-C156 are supported by titration curve data (Figure 4b), phasor analysis (Figure 4c,e), and methodological validation. The adaptation of the Celli et al. method is appropriate and well-documented. The consistency between time-domain and phase-domain approaches (C104) validates the analytical framework. The phasor clouds lying on the calibration trajectory (C101) confirms the validity of the approach in vivo.

results.result: Measurements in non-fluorescent wild-type mice showed phasor clouds located around position (0,0), indicating that the signal mainly originates from detector noise rather than autofluorescence.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 is supported by control measurements in wild-type mice (Figure 4g). This negative control is important for validating that the measured signals in YellowCaB mice are specific to TN-XXL expression rather than tissue autofluorescence.

results.result: At day 8 post-immunization, B cells were classified into five populations based on location and fluorescence. FLIM analysis revealed that calcium concentrations fluctuate in all B cell populations, with most cells maintaining low average calcium concentrations. However, calcium-intermediate and calcium-high subsets were identified among antigen-specific cells and plasma blasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C112 are supported by experimental design (Figure 5a), imaging data (Figure 5b), and bulk analysis (Figure 5c, Video 2,3). The classification scheme is clearly described, and the identification of calcium-high populations is well-documented. The observation of high calcium in plasma blasts (C112-C113) is noted as unexpected given current understanding of BCR downregulation.

results.result: Calcium concentration distributions depend on BCR specificity rather than spatial location within the imaging volume. Antigen-specific populations show higher fluctuation than non-specific cells. Calcium values exceeding the TN-XXL dynamic range (>857 nM) were recorded in all subsets, but most frequently in intrafollicular and extrafollicular antigen-specific B cells. Heterogeneity increases progressively from non-specific B cells through activated GC B cells to plasma blasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 are supported by comparative analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and time-resolved tracking (Figure 5d). The conclusion about BCR specificity-dependent rather than location-dependent calcium distributions (C114) is well-supported. The progressive heterogeneity observation (C118) is a reasonable inference from the comparative data across B cell subsets.

results.result: Antigen-specific GC B cells significantly upregulate cytoplasmic calcium within minutes after intravenous NP-BSA injection. BTK inhibition with ibrutinib abrogates this calcium increase and appears to downregulate baseline signals, demonstrating that BCR-mediated calcium increase substantially contributes to calcium heterogeneity in the GC.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124, C170-C171 are supported by intravital FLIM measurements before and after antigen injection (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The ibrutinib control experiment (C123-C124) provides strong evidence for BCR-dependence of the calcium response. The sample size (3 mice per condition) is modest but adequate for this type of intravital imaging experiment.

results.result: LPS/IL-4-cultured B1-8 plasma blasts show increased calcium after NP-BSA addition in vitro, suggesting that antigen stimulation remains possible in at least a proportion of differentiated B cells. This finding is consistent with reports of residual BCR signaling in antibody-secreting cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126, C182-C183 are supported by in vitro measurements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) and citation to Pinto et al. (2013). The observation challenges the prevailing view that plasma cells completely downregulate surface BCR (C184). However, the authors appropriately note that experiments were done in short-lived plasma blasts, not long-lived plasma cells (C185).

results.result: Extrafollicular B cells in the subcapsular sinus (SCS) have multiple contact sites with SCS macrophages (SCSM). B cells in direct contact with SCSM show calcium concentrations more than doubled compared to non-contacting cells, with calcium positively correlated with contact strength. Single-cell tracking reveals that calcium increases are a direct consequence of B cell-SCSM contacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C133, C189 are supported by intravital imaging (Figure 6b, Video 4), bulk analysis (Figure 6c top), and single-cell tracking (Figure 6c bottom). The correlation between SCSM contact and calcium elevation is clearly demonstrated. However, the causality claim (C132) and the attribution to antigenic activation (C133) are inferences rather than direct demonstrations, as acknowledged by the authors' use of 'presumably.'

results.result: High cytoplasmic calcium levels in medullary cord plasma blasts are unlikely to result from chemokine-induced signaling, as CXCL12 stimulation produced only minor calcium increases in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C119, C188 are supported by CXCL12 stimulation experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d). This negative result helps rule out chemokine signaling as the primary source of high calcium in plasma blasts, though it doesn't definitively identify the actual source.

results.result: A novel transgenic reporter system and FLIM-based image processing approach was developed that enables quantification of absolute cytosolic calcium concentrations in B cells. The FRET-based TN-XXL sensor is stable in moving, proliferating, and differentiating lymphocytes, with suitable sensitivity and fast reversibility. This represents the first determination of absolute B cell calcium concentrations during the GC reaction in living mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C149, C157, C178 represent the core methodological and conceptual advance of the study. The development is well-supported by comprehensive validation experiments throughout the manuscript. The claim of being 'first' (C178) is supported by the literature review showing previous studies used ex vivo analysis or non-reversible reporters (C137-C138). The technical advantages of FLIM over ratiometric methods are well-established.

results.result: Calcium in activated B cells is highly dynamic, and activation introduces persistent calcium heterogeneity to the B cell lineage. Different patterns of calcium fluctuation exist across B cell subsets, with heterogeneity evident in extrafollicular B cells and plasma blasts. Plasma blasts reach the highest calcium concentrations within the B cell compartment. BCR specificity and differentiation state are closely related to distinct degrees of calcium heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C36-C37, C120, C179-C181 represent the major biological findings of the study. These are well-supported by comprehensive FLIM measurements across multiple B cell subsets (Figures 5, 6). The progressive heterogeneity from naive to activated to differentiated B cells is clearly documented. The high calcium in plasma blasts (C181) is particularly notable and well-supported by the data.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on calcium signaling in B cells, FRET-FLIM methodology, and the biological context of germinal center reactions. These claims establish the scientific rationale and cite relevant prior work.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C2, C8-C31, C89-C96, C134-C145, C153-C154, C160, C162-C166, C173-C177, C192-C193) are primarily literature-based background claims supported by appropriate citations. They establish the context for the study and justify the methodological approach. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of prior work are reasonable.

results.result: The manuscript includes several speculative interpretations about mechanisms underlying observed calcium dynamics, including BCR internalization, calcium storage capacity, metabolic stress in high-calcium cells, signal integration thresholds, and future research directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C61, C113, C159, C161, C169, C172, C186, C190, C195 are explicitly or implicitly speculative. While these speculations are reasonable given the data and are appropriately qualified by the authors (using terms like 'probably,' 'might,' 'could,' 'possibly'), they represent hypotheses rather than demonstrated findings. These would require additional experiments to confirm.

results.result: The phasor approach circumvents problems of multiexponential fluorescence decays encountered when measuring two-fluorophore FRET-based calcium indicators in tissue.
results.evaluation: Claim C151 is supported by the demonstrated application of phasor analysis to the complex in vivo FLIM data. The advantage of phasor analysis for handling multiexponential decays is well-established in the literature (C95) and is validated by the successful application in this study.

results.result: TLR signaling can attenuate calcium flux in stimulated B cells, while CD40 can either attenuate or augment the calcium response depending on conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C168 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2. The bidirectional effects of CD40 (C168) are clearly documented, though the mechanistic basis and determinants of the different outcomes remain to be elucidated (C169).

results.result: The ability of B cells to collect sequential signals is a key factor enabling observation of repeated and partially sustained calcium elevation in the cytoplasm.
results.evaluation: Claim C158 is supported by the repeated stimulation experiments (Figure 2b) and the in vivo observations of calcium dynamics during FDC contacts (Figure 3d). This represents an important functional insight about B cell calcium signaling.

results.result: The YellowCaB system provides a tool for measuring calcium as a universal cellular messenger integrating signals from various pathways. The authors have previously applied phasor-FLIM of NAD(P)H fluorescence for metabolic mapping in cell cultures.
results.evaluation: Claims C191, C194 are supported by the comprehensive validation of the YellowCaB system throughout the manuscript and by citation to Leben et al. (2019) for the NAD(P)H work. These claims appropriately summarize the utility and potential of the developed system.
